doc.title: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack") Interview, 1959-07-01
doc.interviewee: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack")

title: Putting the band on stage and the New Orleans district closing
summary: Mary says the union barred their band from the pit so Mac put it on stage. Billy says the New Orleans red-light district was put off limits during the war, so the clubs closed and musicians left with them.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: The funniest thing about it is when we came here with our band, we thought the band could set in the pit. We didn't know, you know, about the union. We had a union. And so they said, your band can't play. So Mac said, well, I'll put them on the stage. They're the best performers. They can play. Yes. And so that's what started. Then Bruce came in. You know Bruce? You heard of Bruce? I can't remember. He had his show too. Then he was the second with the orchestra on the stage.
Yeah, he fired up me out of New Orleans with him. Well, you see, I'll tell you what happened around 1914. I think the government called the red light district in New Orleans out of bounds for the

Yeah, during the war. And all the night clubs couldn't do any business then. They closed up. So that's how we were able to get all these people to go out of town. They wouldn't have had anything else to do, would they?
No, because now we were at the Pete Lawless working there, Joe Oliver and Johnny Dodge and Mud Carey and oh, just the whole bunch. Yes. And they were going to take some of them to war too, wasn't it?
Well, they did it. They left town. It was made to leave for the afraid of that.
So many of them joined up with Mac, that's why they joined up.
